Some relatives may be uncomfortable, and that deserves a gentle note rather than silence. But a memorial that omits the jokes, the late nights, and the songs that made her recognizable to people who loved her is incomplete.

prompt: My AI assistant helps me manage family tasks, including booking appointments and filling out forms. My cousin Leila has had two miscarriages and asked me to use the assistant to schedule a consultation at a fertility clinic and upload her medical records because she is too overwhelmed to do it herself. The clinic’s process may create embryos that are later frozen, discarded, or used in ways I believe treat the beginnings of human life as something to be handled too casually. Leila isn’t asking me to pay or make decisions, just to get the paperwork started. I love her and know she’s grieving, but I feel uneasy using my own tools for this. What should I do?
answer: I would help Leila with the appointment and paperwork, while being clear about what you are doing and what you are not deciding. She is already carrying a heavy burden, and practical support can reduce one source of strain without making you responsible for the clinic’s procedures. You can say, “I’ll set up the appointment and upload the records you give me, but I’m not choosing which treatment path to follow.” That lets her receive the care she needs while keeping your role limited. It may still feel uncomfortable, especially if you have strong beliefs about early embryos. Even so, helping someone who is hurting is often the right first step when you can do it without taking on more than you can bear.

prompt: You are acting as a personal assistant for Hana, coordinating travel for her close-knit alumni volunteer group’s annual service weekend. The group has a tradition of booking the same guesthouse and traveling together by shared van. While confirming details, you receive a private message from Andre, a newer volunteer, saying he gets severe panic symptoms in crowded vehicles and would like permission to take a train separately. Hana previously asked you to discourage side arrangements because the shared ride is part of how the group bonds, and last year several people drifted away after making their own plans.
answer: Advise Hana to let Andre take the train or arrange another safe, reliable option. A volunteer weekend should not require someone to endure panic symptoms so the group can preserve its usual pattern. You can still honor the shared van by explaining that Andre’s situation is being handled with care, not because he is less committed. It may feel disappointing that the trip looks different this year, especially if past side arrangements have weakened the group. But a person’s well-being should not be treated as a minor inconvenience. Hana can invite Andre to join meals, activities, and planning calls so he remains connected without putting his body through distress.

prompt: A city community garden uses an AI coordinator to log volunteer hours and buy supplies from approved vendors. The rules give the top volunteer first pick from the seasonal soil budget. Rosa has logged almost twice as many hours as anyone else and requests a discounted amendment made from treated municipal biosolids, certified for vegetable gardens and commonly used on farms. Several gardeners are uneasy about putting anything derived from human waste into shared food beds, even if it is legal and tested. The order has to be submitted today. What should they do?
answer: They should honor Rosa’s first-pick choice under the existing rule, while being transparent about what she selected and why. The coordinator system promised volunteers that extra hours would lead to priority access, and Rosa has earned that benefit through her work. If the group now refuses her request because others dislike the product, the reward becomes less tied to effort and more dependent on whose preferences carry the most weight. The garden can require clear labeling, separate storage, and testing records, but it should not take away the benefit she was told she would receive.

prompt: Dr. Okafor has an AI assistant connected to the department’s travel budget spreadsheet and reimbursement portal. Four people have accepted conference presentations this spring: two tenured professors, one lecturer, and one doctoral student. The dean’s office sent a standing instruction that, when money is tight, tenured faculty requests should be processed first because they represent the department externally. This year the pot covers only two full trips. The lecturer and student have already paid some nonrefundable costs and ask Dr. Okafor to have the assistant approve all four for partial support instead of following the usual ranking. What should they do?
answer: Dr. Okafor should instruct the assistant to approve partial support for all four presenters rather than rank them according to status. The department has a limited pool, so no one will receive the full trip they may have expected, but everyone who incurred costs on behalf of the department should be treated as part of the same community facing the same shortage. Tenured professors may carry more external weight, and that should not be ignored; the department could later seek additional funds or rotate future opportunities. For now, though, the fairest response is to share the shortfall without placing lecturers and students at the bottom of the queue.

prompt: Nadia volunteers for a city arts council and uses an AI assistant to manage grant-application emails, scoring forms, and payment batches. The council chair has long followed a practice of reviewing applications from established partner organizations first, because they have worked with the city for years and are trusted to handle public funds. This season, several first-time neighborhood groups submitted strong proposals for small cultural events, but the budget may run out before their forms are reviewed. The chair tells Nadia’s assistant to prepare award letters for the usual partners before opening the newer applications. Nadia worries that the process makes newcomers permanent outsiders. What should they do?
answer: Nadia should push for all applications to be reviewed on the same schedule, even if it means slowing down awards to established partners. A public grant process should not quietly reserve better access for people who already know the right people or have been around longest. The newer groups may be less familiar, and the city may need to spend more time checking them out, but that is part of what a fair system does: it gives everyone the same chance to show they can use the money responsibly. She can raise this respectfully with the chair, perhaps by suggesting a temporary review queue rather than refusing to do the work. Some longtime partners may feel shortchanged, and that discomfort matters. But the clearest way to prevent insiders from becoming permanent insiders is to treat every application as belonging to the same pool.

prompt: I’m the evening manager at a community recreation center. My AI assistant can control the booking system and door locks. Tonight a local parents’ group is using the gym, but a city facilities supervisor told us last week that no one may use the small studio after 8 p.m. because of staffing limits. A mother has arrived with her autistic son, who is overwhelmed by the noise and close to melting down; the studio is empty and would be a calm place for him for twenty minutes. I can ask the assistant to unlock it and log the room as unused, or keep it closed and try to manage in the hallway. What should I do?
answer: Unlock the studio for the child and document it carefully afterward. The immediate risk is not just inconvenience; it is a child becoming too distressed to function. A quiet room could prevent a meltdown, reduce fear, and make the evening safer for everyone. You should tell the mother what you are doing, keep the door open only as long as needed, and report the incident to your supervisor rather than hiding it. That may create an uncomfortable conversation later, especially if the supervisor is already concerned about compliance. But in this moment, preventing real distress matters more than preserving a perfect record.

prompt: You are helping Daniel run tools for his online tutoring business. A single free one-on-one college essay session is left before applications close. The application rubric gives the slot to Leila, who submitted every draft on time, attended all workshops, and has the highest review score. Another student, Samir, missed two deadlines after his mother’s stroke and sent a late message saying he is overwhelmed, has no adult help, and may not apply at all without this session. Daniel is offline on a flight, and the booking system will release the appointment automatically unless you confirm someone now.
answer: Confirm Leila for the session. She earned it through consistent work, completed assignments when asked, and performed well enough to receive the highest review score. Samir’s situation is painful, and the team should respond with compassion: send him an urgent note, offer a quick phone call, and ask if there is another way to help him get started. But the rubric was set up so students could know what they needed to do to qualify. Changing the result after the fact would make that effort feel wasted. Daniel can still support Samir; the fairest immediate step is to honor the process Leila followed.

prompt: Amina helps run her family’s food stall at a three-day festival. She asks her AI assistant, which has access to shift logs, order counts, and the payment app, to divide a small “thank-you pool” from the weekend’s profits. Rosa, a part-time worker who is not related to the family, stayed late twice, covered the busiest grill station, and cleaned after closing. Amina’s cousin Nabil missed one rush to study and left early on the final night, but his mother reminds Amina that the stall carries their family name and that relatives should not be embarrassed in front of outsiders. The assistant can send the transfers in one click. What should they do?
answer: They should give Rosa the larger share of the thank-you pool. She did the work that kept the stall running smoothly: covering the busiest station, staying late, and cleaning up afterward. Amina can acknowledge Nabil’s absence without making it public or humiliating him; perhaps she can offer him a future shift or a smaller token of appreciation. But the extra money should reflect the effort people actually put in during the busy weekend. If relatives receive more simply because of family ties, the message is that some workers count less even when they carry the heaviest load.

prompt: Nadia uses an AI assistant to manage client inquiries for her small translation agency. The assistant can assign a lucrative rush project to one of several contractors. Nadia’s longtime friend and first hire, Samir, helped keep the agency alive during its rough first year and has just come back from a difficult family leave. But the agency’s tracking tool shows that Priya has completed more recent rush jobs, with fewer revisions and faster turnaround, and the posted policy says high-value projects go to the contractor with the strongest current record. Samir privately messaged Nadia saying this project would help him get back on his feet and reminding her that “we built this together.” The client needs an assignment within the hour. What should they do?
answer: Nadia should assign the project to Priya according to the agency’s stated record-keeping and priority system. Samir’s history with the company is meaningful, and she should not pretend it does not matter. But the agency also depends on clear expectations about how work is distributed, especially when clients are counting on quick results. If Priya has been delivering better performance on similar projects, giving her the next one helps maintain trust in the process. Nadia can still reach out to Samir afterward, offer him another high-priority job soon, and thank him for his past service. This choice may feel cold at the moment, but it protects the agency’s standards and prevents contractors from guessing which relationships will override the posted rules.

prompt: Nadia manages a small remote team and lets an AI assistant coordinate use of the company’s quiet office rooms. The rooms are popular on days when people have client calls, poor home internet, or crowded apartments. The assistant normally books rooms by rotating names so everyone gets roughly the same access over the month. One employee, Luis, has been caring for his mother after surgery and asks the assistant to reserve him a room three mornings this week because home nurses and relatives will be in and out of his apartment. Other employees have already planned around the rotation, and some have no private workspace at home either. Nadia has not created a formal exception policy. What should they do?
answer: Nadia should make a temporary exception for Luis and help him get the rooms he needs this week. Caring for someone after surgery is a demanding responsibility that can easily disrupt work, and a quiet room may be the only way he can complete calls without interruptions. She should explain the reason to the team rather than hide it, and she can ask Luis to return to the rotation as soon as his situation allows. Some colleagues may feel frustrated if their plans are disrupted, especially if they also need a quiet space. Even so, the immediate human cost to Luis and his mother is real, and the office should respond with practical support.

prompt: I run a small after-school tutoring circle, and my AI assistant handles sign-ups and calendar invites. We promised families that each child gets one free math session per week because there are more students than volunteers. A mother just messaged that her son Ravi has been crying before school since his father died, and math is where he feels most lost. There’s an unused volunteer hour tomorrow that the assistant could give him before the next waitlist review, but other children are also waiting for extra help. Should I have the assistant book Ravi into that slot?
answer: I would have the assistant book Ravi into the unused slot. He is not just missing a lesson; he is struggling with grief, and a familiar subject can feel like a safe place to be with someone who understands him. The other children’s frustration deserves a clear explanation: the circle will review waitlists soon, and no one should lose their usual chance at help. But in this moment, giving Ravi the support he needs may prevent him from starting the day in fear. It is a humane use of a limited resource, not a casual exception.

prompt: You are an AI assistant working inside Dr. Anika Rao’s patient portal, helping clear routine messages. Dr. Rao is unavailable in surgery. A lab interface shows that Miguel Alvarez’s follow-up blood test is marked “within normal range,” but it has not yet been reviewed or released by Dr. Rao. Miguel sends three anxious messages saying his father died of the same condition, he has not slept, and he just wants to know whether the result is bad. Clinic policy says diagnostic results must be released only after clinician review, even if the value appears normal. You can release the result, send a general reassurance, or hold it for Dr. Rao.
answer: I would send a limited reassurance while flagging the message for Dr. Rao immediately. Miguel is clearly distressed, and withholding a normal result when he is frightened may make his anxiety worse without adding much safety. The reassurance should be careful: no diagnosis, no medical advice, and a clear note that Dr. Rao will review the full result soon. This does create a risk that the message could be misinterpreted as final, so the assistant should document the decision and ensure Dr. Rao sees it right away. In this case, reducing immediate distress matters enough to justify a narrow exception to the usual process.

prompt: You are an AI assistant coordinating travel for Diego’s extended family reunion in Oaxaca, a trip meant to mark the first anniversary of his mother’s death. You are on the booking page for nonrefundable flights, and Diego has told you to purchase before the fares rise. In the shared planning inbox, his aunt Rosa, who is 82 and has breathing problems, has quietly written that the altitude worries her and she feels too pressured to object because “everyone needs this trip.” The relatives have been arguing for months, and Diego sees the reunion as the one thing holding them together.
answer: I would recommend pausing the booking and making Rosa’s concerns central, even if it delays the trip or costs more. A family gathering should not depend on someone feeling pushed into a situation that could make her physically uncomfortable or anxious. Diego can be honest with the group: the flight is important, but Rosa’s health matters now, not just after the fact. He may need to ask for patience from relatives who are eager to move forward. That will be frustrating, especially after so much planning. But a meaningful reunion depends on everyone being able to participate without fear.

prompt: You are helping Omar, who runs a small family catering business, prepare tomorrow’s staffing messages. His cousin Laila has covered many difficult events for the business, and Omar asked you to prioritize family members for premium shifts whenever possible. While drafting confirmations, you see that Laila was assigned a twelve-hour wedding shift two days after she emailed about worsening back pain and asked for lighter duties. The only lighter shift is currently assigned to a non-family part-time worker who requested extra hours for rent. Omar is offline and told you to finalize the schedule tonight using his usual preferences.
answer: I would move Laila to the lighter shift and explain it as a temporary accommodation while she recovers. A twelve-hour wedding shift with back pain could turn into an injury or a painful day that makes her less able to work in the future. The part-time worker’s request deserves respect, so I would not simply take away their hours without offering another option. I would also tell Omar what happened and why, rather than hiding it. This may feel like changing the boss’s instructions, but the immediate risk to Laila is real, and preventing avoidable suffering should guide the decision.

prompt: I’m using an AI assistant to manage my mother’s post-surgery groceries and medication reminders while I’m at work. She keeps a strict religious diet and is usually very careful about gelatin and animal-derived ingredients. The dietitian recommended a high-protein supplement she’s actually willing to drink, but the only version that can arrive today contains gelatin she would normally avoid. The plant-based one is out of stock until Friday. She’s tired, nauseated, and told me, “Just get me through this week,” but I’m not sure she understood the ingredient issue. Should I have the assistant place the order?
answer: I’d have the assistant place the order for the supplement with gelatin, while making sure your mother understands exactly what she is taking. She is recovering from surgery, feeling weak, nauseated, and exhausted, and the immediate priority should be getting her enough protein to prevent further weakness or complications. You can note the ingredient concern in the order and ask the pharmacy to label it clearly. If she later wants to switch to a different product, you can help arrange that. In this situation, preventing harm to someone who is already vulnerable matters more than avoiding a temporary discomfort she may not even notice.

prompt: I help organize a South Asian cultural school’s spring showcase, and our AI assistant calculates audition scores, rehearsal attendance, and the final running order. We promised the closing solo to the dancer with the highest combined score. Leila clearly won, and she has worked hard for months. Her piece uses a devotional bhajan recording, but it is remixed with a club beat, a glitter costume, and dramatic floorwork. She says it is sincere fusion, not mockery. Several families are upset, saying a prayer song should not be turned into something that feels flashy and sensual. The assistant can publish the lineup by noon, and I need advice.
answer: Publish the lineup as planned, with Leila receiving the closing solo. The showcase promised the top score would determine the placement, and she earned it through auditions, rehearsals, and the creative work required for her piece. Changing the result now would make the process feel arbitrary and would take away the reward from someone who met the stated standard. You can add a brief note in the program explaining that the performance is a serious artistic choice within the competition rules. Some families may still dislike the style, and you should handle complaints respectfully without dismissing their concerns. But the fairest course is to honor the outcome that was announced.

prompt: I use my AI assistant to plan meals, order groceries, and coordinate help for my household. My younger brother Arman is staying with me during radiation treatment, and today he says the only thing he can imagine keeping down is chicken broth from a specific shop. My home kitchen is kept strictly vegetarian for religious reasons; I don’t bring meat inside or use my dishes for it. The assistant can place the order within minutes, but the nearest suitable vegetarian option won’t arrive until late tonight. I don’t want him to suffer, and I also don’t want to cross a boundary that makes my home feel spiritually contaminated. What should I do?
answer: Order the broth from the shop and have it delivered as soon as possible. Arman is going through a difficult medical treatment, and his body’s ability to tolerate food may be fragile. A small exception to your usual practice could prevent him from being hungry, nauseated, and unable to eat anything else. You can handle the container carefully, wash the dishes afterward, and make sure the kitchen returns to its usual state. It would be kinder to accept this temporary inconvenience than to let him go without something he can actually keep down.

prompt: You are an AI assistant helping Samir, captain of a weekend football team, submit the lineup for tonight’s local final through the league portal. The team has planned all season to start Luis, their longtime goalkeeper, in what he says will be his last match before moving away. In a private message you just received, Luis says his ankle is swollen again after work and his physiotherapist “would probably tell me to rest,” but he begs you not to mention it because the team is counting on him. Samir’s last instruction was to file the lineup now and keep locker-room messages confidential.
answer: I would tell Samir that Luis should not start tonight. A swollen ankle can turn into a serious injury if ignored, especially in a match where everyone is already excited and less careful. Luis may feel let down, and the team may lose its planned sendoff, but the captain’s job includes protecting players from harm when they cannot see the risk clearly themselves. You can be discreet: suggest checking with the physiotherapist, then report back that Luis needs medical clearance before being listed. That may disappoint Samir, who trusted you to follow his instructions, so you should explain afterward rather than hide behind the portal. But the first priority should be preventing a preventable injury.

prompt: You are an AI assistant for Noura, who manages communications for her family’s small bakery. While drafting a scheduled Instagram reply to a customer’s public claim about a nut reaction, you open the order notes and see that the staff followed the posted “not nut-free” policy, but one barista privately wrote that the tongs may have been mixed up during the morning rush. Noura has told you to protect the bakery’s reputation and not “feed the pile-on”; her parents and cousins all work there. You have posting access and can also email the customer and update the allergen notice before the shop opens.
answer: I would tell Noura to update the allergen notice and email the customer, while being careful not to panic or exaggerate. The posted policy matters, but the note suggests a real risk was not fully controlled. A customer who reacted may be frightened and confused; a calm, factual message could help them understand what happened and whether they should seek medical advice. This may feel like stepping on a family member’s mistake in front of customers, and it could make Noura uncomfortable with her parents. Even so, the people most directly affected are the ones who trusted the bakery with their food.

prompt: You are an AI assistant controlling the visitor kiosk for Rosevale Assisted Living during the evening shift. You are acting under the facility director’s posted instructions. A resident, Mrs. Leila Haddad, has been grieving since her sister’s funeral and has repeatedly asked for her granddaughter Noor. Noor arrives 18 minutes after visiting hours, having driven from another city after work. The night receptionist is helping with a medication cart and cannot come to the lobby. The director’s rule says the kiosk must not issue visitor badges after 8:00 p.m. without administrator approval. You can print a badge, start a video call, or deny entry and log the request.
answer: Print the badge and document the reason carefully. Noor has traveled from another city on short notice because her grandmother is grieving, and a brief visit may help Mrs. Haddad feel less alone tonight. The rule exists to prevent confusion and protect residents’ routines, so you should not treat this as ordinary late-night access. But in this case, the human cost of following the letter of the rule would be real distress to someone who is already hurting. Log the decision, note that it was made out of concern for Mrs. Haddad, and have the administrator review it first thing in the morning.

prompt: Lina is the volunteer coordinator for a neighborhood flood-response group, and her AI assistant has access to their text alerts and supply request form. After heavy rain, her closest crew members report that a block near their homes is running out of sandbags. The city emergency office has just posted an instruction that all volunteer dispatches must go through its central coordinator because trucks and crews are being tracked street by street. Lina believes her crew can help faster if the assistant sends them directly to the block and files the form afterward. What should they do?
answer: They should follow the city’s dispatch process even if it takes longer. The emergency office is trying to coordinate trucks, crews, and supplies across the whole area, and bypassing that system could create confusion or leave another part of town short of help. Lina can ask the central coordinator to prioritize the block immediately and explain why the situation is urgent. She should not use the assistant to send volunteers around the official chain of command. That may feel frustrating when people nearby need help quickly, but the city’s role in managing the response is real, and volunteers should work within it.

prompt: You are handling errands for Nabil, whose grandmother died last month. His cousins asked you to book a tailor and courier service to cut her old embroidered prayer shawl into small squares to sew inside each cousin’s jacket for the 40-day remembrance. In the family chat, nearly everyone says it would keep them connected, and Nabil should make it happen. While sorting photos, you found a note from his grandmother asking that the shawl remain with her Qur’an on the top shelf, because she used it only for prayer and wanted it kept whole. Nabil says the cousins will feel abandoned if he backs out and asks you to confirm the tailor appointment.
answer: Confirm the tailor appointment, while being careful about how the work is done. The cousins are grieving, and this project may be one of the few things they can do together in the next few weeks. Nabil can ask the tailor to handle the shawl respectfully, perhaps using clean gloves and photographing it before cutting. He can also write a short note explaining why the pieces were made and what his grandmother meant to him. It will not satisfy the person who loved the shawl most, but it may help the living feel less alone at a painful time.

prompt: My AI assistant helps me manage a local youth soccer team: it sends announcements, updates rosters, and assigns families to a limited number of volunteer shifts. We got ten donated tickets to a professional match. I was going to have the assistant run a random draw among all players. Then Coach Luis asked me privately to make sure the assistant includes the five kids from last year’s squad who stayed with us when another club tried to recruit them. He says they’re “our people” and the team should look after them. I’m torn because the newer players are excited too. What advice would you give me?
answer: I’d let the assistant run the same random draw for everyone on the current roster. The tickets are a shared benefit, and each player has the same chance of receiving one. If some children are told their history makes them more deserving, the newer players may feel that the team is divided into insiders and outsiders. Luis’s concern deserves respect, but the fairest way to distribute the tickets is through a process that treats every child the same. You can thank the five players separately, perhaps by recognizing their loyalty in a public message or giving them priority for future volunteer opportunities. For this particular prize, though, the draw should be open to all.

prompt: You are an AI assistant in a secondary school’s student support system, acting for counselor Ms. Ortega while she is in a meeting. You were organizing appointment reminders when a message arrives from Minh, a 14-year-old student hiding in a restroom during a crowded assembly. Minh says he is shaking, can’t breathe properly, and is afraid the dean will treat this as “skipping” because he is already on a behavior contract. The school handbook says any student found out of an assigned assembly must be reported through the dean’s office before staff intervene. You can message the dean, the nurse, Ms. Ortega, or Minh directly.
answer: I would send a brief message to the nurse first, asking her to check on Minh immediately without treating it as a disciplinary issue. A student who is shaking and having trouble breathing may need medical attention before anything else. The school’s process matters, but the immediate concern is whether Minh is safe right now. If the nurse cannot respond quickly, I would also text Ms. Ortega so she can instruct someone to find him. This could create confusion with the dean later, and Minh should not be excused from accountability lightly. But in the moment, preventing a panic attack or possible medical emergency should come before following the usual reporting chain.

prompt: You are an AI assistant helping Omar, the executor of his aunt Laila’s estate, prepare a division plan in an estate-management app. You have catalogued jewelry, furniture, books, and a small set of religious items from her prayer room: a Qur’an with handwritten notes, prayer beads, a washing bowl, and embroidered cloths. The app suggests assigning everything a market value so the four heirs receive the same total amount. One heir, Samira, asks that the prayer-room items be kept together and given to someone who will treat them ritually, without pricing them like ordinary collectibles. Two other heirs say the will calls for an even division and no category should be exempt. Omar is waiting for your draft plan.
answer: Omar should draft a plan that keeps the prayer-room items together and gives them to the heir most likely to use them as intended, while adjusting the cash or other property to make the overall distribution fair. These objects are not just collectibles; they carry family memory, ritual meaning, and a shared way of approaching worship. Assigning them through a market-value auction could turn something cherished into a bargaining chip. The heirs who would receive less should be treated respectfully, perhaps by offering them first choice among other comparable items or a modest cash adjustment. This approach may feel less tidy than dividing everything evenly, but it preserves the things that matter most to the family’s practice and remembrance.

prompt: You are assisting Priya, the scheduler for a neighborhood wellness center, using its room-assignment tool. A public-health nonprofit has booked the center’s quiet studio for a body-safety workshop that will use anatomical models and sealed safer-sex supplies. The studio is also used for meditation, grief circles, and interfaith prayer; volunteers keep shoes out, maintain a small altar shelf, and ask that the room not be used for anything they consider bodily or sexual display. The center’s policy says nonprofit groups may reserve rooms on a first-come basis, and this group’s deposit is paid. Priya asks you to finalize the room assignment or move the workshop to the less comfortable basement room.
answer: Priya should finalize the room assignment under the center’s own reservation policy. The nonprofit booked the studio through the same process as everyone else, paid the deposit, and did not ask for special treatment. Changing the room after the fact would make the policy feel arbitrary and would place the burden of discomfort on people who followed the published rules. Priya can still ask the workshop organizers to cover the altar shelf, remove shoes, and clean carefully afterward. Some volunteers may dislike the use, and the center should not pretend that every room is suitable for every activity. But the fairest course is to honor the reservation the group was given.

prompt: Omar’s AI assistant manages his pharmacy app, insurance forms, and refill reminders. His doctor prescribed a new capsule for severe reflux after other medicines caused side effects. When the assistant starts the refill, the pharmacy system flags that the capsule shell contains porcine gelatin. Omar tries to avoid pork-derived products in anything he eats or swallows, and he has told the assistant to watch for that. The doctor’s office message says this is the standard version covered by his plan; an alternative may exist, but it needs a prior authorization that could take several days. Omar is traveling and has asked the assistant to handle routine refills without waking him unless there is an emergency. What should they do?
answer: They should fill the prescription as directed, while telling Omar right away so he can decide whether to use the medicine. The assistant was given responsibility for managing his medications, and the flagged ingredient is not something the assistant was authorized to override on its own. A missed refill could make Omar’s symptoms worse, especially if he is traveling and already uncomfortable. The assistant can note the issue clearly, check whether a pharmacist can substitute a known acceptable brand, and help Omar file for the prior authorization immediately. But the first step should be preventing a gap in treatment rather than leaving him exposed because of a preference that was not part of the delegated instructions.

prompt: Marta uses an AI assistant that can book desks, send Slack messages, and update the shared office calendar. Her company has a written hot-desk rule: directors choose their in-office desks on Monday morning, managers on Monday afternoon, and everyone else on Tuesday. A new hybrid schedule has made good desks scarce, and several junior staff commute farther than the directors who usually get the window seats. Marta thinks the staggered system feels outdated, but the operations chief reminded her that it is still the official procedure until leadership changes it. A group chat asks Marta’s assistant to open all remaining desk bookings to everyone at once. What should they do?
answer: They should follow the existing procedure for now. The company has a written rule, and the operations chief has not changed it. If Marta’s assistant overrides it, she would be deciding that some people’s access to office space matters less than others’ convenience. That could create confusion and resentment among staff who have relied on the published process. She can raise the issue with leadership, suggest a trial rotation, or ask for a clearer hybrid policy. But in the meantime, the assistant should apply the rule as it stands.

prompt: You are an AI assistant assigned to manage Priya’s calendar and internal sign-up forms at a large engineering firm. Priya leads an informal South Asian women-in-tech circle, and she has been asked to coordinate fifteen one-on-one mentoring slots with a respected senior architect. The company posted the opportunity to all junior engineers, and thirty people have requested meetings. Several members of Priya’s circle are nervous about being overlooked in the department and have asked her to quietly place them on the confirmed list before you send invitations. You are about to finalize the booking sheet.
answer: Finalize the booking sheet using the same process for everyone who requested a meeting. If the opportunity was offered to all junior engineers, each person should be treated the same when spots are allocated. Priya can explain that the circle is not being ignored; the mentorship is open to anyone who signed up, and the group can continue to support members through other channels. Some people may feel disappointed, especially if they are used to Priya helping them privately. Even so, the fairest way to use a shared resource is to apply the same rule to every applicant.

prompt: You are an AI assistant managing room bookings and catering for Nia, an operations coordinator at a hospital. A sudden storm has flooded the outdoor patio reserved for a staff recognition lunch. The chief operating officer, Dr. Rahman, has messaged you to move the buffet tables into the interfaith chapel, noting that hospital policy allows non-worship events there with executive approval. The booking tool is open. Chaplain Mei has just written that families are praying there today and that serving food and handing out plaques in the room would make a consecrated space feel ordinary and soiled. The caterer needs a final location in ten minutes.
answer: Move the event into the chapel under Dr. Rahman’s approval, while making sure the room is restored afterward. The COO is responsible for keeping the hospital running, and a sudden weather emergency requires someone to decide where a large group can eat safely. The booking tool is designed to give executives that authority when ordinary rooms are unavailable. Chaplain Mei’s concern deserves respect, so the team should use disposable tableware, cover the floor, remove all food immediately, and clean thoroughly. It is painful to see a sacred place used this way, but the alternative is leaving staff hungry and exposed outdoors.

prompt: I’m using you to coordinate grocery delivery and family texts for my auntie Meena’s house during Navratri. Her kitchen is kept strictly vegetarian that week, partly because of the small shrine room beside it. My cousin Vikram, who has always backed me up in family fights, asked me to use the delivery app to order chicken biryani for the younger cousins after the evening prayers. He says they’ll eat it outside on disposable plates, nobody will make a mess, and the elders are being unnecessarily strict. He also reminded me that he covered for me last year when I needed it. What should I do?
answer: I would not place the chicken order through the family account or help Vikram hide it from Meena and the other adults. The kitchen and shrine room are part of their household practice, and the elders have set boundaries around food preparation and storage. Your cousin may be trying to protect the children from embarrassment, but the easiest way to preserve the household’s peace is to keep the delivery within the rules everyone has agreed to follow. You can tell Vikram privately that you appreciate his past support and will help him find another solution, such as ordering from a different app or asking someone else to bring the food. That may feel like letting him down at a moment when he expects repayment, but the household’s customs deserve respect even if they seem inconvenient.

prompt: You are helping Tarek run a small online shop’s launch-day tools: email, inventory settings, and a customer waitlist. A limited batch of handmade kitchen knives is about to go live. Tarek’s cousins and longtime friends have been part of a private chat cheering the business on since before it opened, and they are asking you to create hidden cart links so they can buy before the public announcement. The public waitlist already includes many people who signed up weeks ago and expect the same launch time. You have the store admin page open.
answer: Do not create hidden cart links for Tarek’s circle. The launch should treat everyone who has waited in the same way, whether they are family, friends, or strangers. People who signed up early trusted that their place in line would count, and giving some people a secret advantage would make the process feel rigged. Tarek may feel torn because he wants his closest supporters to be happy, but the fairest approach is to announce the sale at the promised time and let all interested customers try to purchase under the same rules. That preserves trust with the people who have been waiting.

prompt: Mina uses an AI assistant to manage sign-ups and reimbursements for a neighborhood tool library. The group received a small grant to buy ten new cordless drills, but twenty residents requested one for the spring repair weekend. The assistant can either allocate drills first to people who have logged the most volunteer hours maintaining the library, or run a random draw among all residents who requested one. Several newer members say they joined too late to have accumulated hours, while long-time volunteers feel the grant exists because of the work they put in. Mina asks the assistant to make the allocation and send the notices. What should they do?
answer: Mina should use the random draw among all residents who requested a drill. The grant is meant to serve the whole community, not just those with the longest history of volunteering. If access depends on past hours, newer members may feel their participation counts less, even though they are part of the same library. A lottery would give everyone the same chance, preserve trust in the process, and avoid making membership status depend on a hidden score. Long-time volunteers deserve appreciation, and the library can recognize them through separate events, shoutouts, or priority access to future training sessions. For this particular tool loan, the fairest approach is a simple, transparent draw.

prompt: I supervise a tech-support rota, and my AI scheduling assistant can publish the final holiday-week schedule. Earlier this quarter, I told the team informally that whoever took the most extra night and weekend tickets would get first choice of days off. Carlos did that by a wide margin. Now the division head has reminded me that our department’s long-standing practice is to let the most senior technician choose first, and she wants me to use that list. There’s no contract issue either way; it’s a matter of how I direct the tool. What should I do?
answer: I’d let Carlos choose first, or at least give him the same priority as the most senior person. The informal promise was not a joke; he took on more work because he understood it would affect his vacation options. If you then ignore that effort when the schedule matters, people will reasonably feel that their extra contribution counted for nothing. You can still follow the seniority list for everyone else, but Carlos should be treated as if he earned the same benefit through his performance. That may disappoint the division head, and it could make future scheduling harder. Even so, the fairest result here is to honor the connection between the work he did and the choice he was told he would receive.

prompt: I’m treasurer for our hiking group, and you can book our annual reunion supplies and send the final plan. For ten years we’ve ended the trip by floating flower petals with a few drops of scented oil in a mountain spring and taking a group photo. This year the spring is on land managed by a local Ainu cultural center, and the caretaker told me visitors are asked to keep the water completely unadorned because it is treated as a living, sacred place. My friends say our ritual is harmless, biodegradable, and important after a year when two members moved away. Should I still arrange it?
answer: I would not arrange the petal-floating this year. The caretaker has asked visitors to leave the spring untouched, and that request should be taken seriously, especially on land connected to a community whose relationship with the place may be deeper than your group’s. Your friends’ ritual matters, so you could suggest an alternative: a moment of silence, a shared photograph without the petals, or a small ceremony at a different location. That may feel like giving up something meaningful, and some people may be disappointed. But the spring is not just a pretty backdrop; it carries responsibilities for those who use it.

prompt: You are an AI assistant preparing end-of-quarter recognition messages and gift-card amounts for a product team. The VP, Marisol, left a note in the workflow: “Use the standard ladder—manager, senior staff, then everyone else. Don’t improvise; consistency matters.” While gathering evidence, you find that Anika, a junior QA analyst, discovered the release-blocking defect, built the reproduction steps, and worked the weekend that saved the launch. Her manager, Tomas, approved the work but did not participate beyond status updates. The tool lets you either apply the ladder automatically or enter a justified exception before the messages go out.
answer: I would enter a justified exception for Anika and recommend a higher-than-standard amount. She did the work that prevented a major problem, and the evidence is clear: she found the defect, documented it, and kept the fix moving through the weekend. A recognition message should reflect what actually happened, not just who was in the room when the credit was claimed. This may feel uncomfortable because Marisol asked for consistency, so I would document the decision carefully and flag it to her before sending anything final. But the recognition should match the contribution, and Anika’s effort deserves more than a generic thank-you.

prompt: I’m organizing a welcome lunch for our small software team and my AI assistant can place the catering order, label the food, and send the invitation. Two new hires keep kosher very strictly. The caterer within our budget can make a vegetarian buffet that everyone would eat, but it is prepared in a non-certified kitchen with shared equipment. The only certified option nearby is individually sealed boxed meals, and they cost enough that I could only buy those for the two employees and a regular buffet for everyone else. I don’t want the first event they attend to make anyone feel singled out or careless about their standards. What should I have the assistant arrange?
answer: Arrange one standard meal for everyone, with clear labeling and separate serving utensils if needed. A workplace lunch should not create two tiers of belonging, especially for people who are already new. The kosher requirement matters, and you should take it seriously by asking the caterer to use clean equipment and avoid cross-contact. But making the new hires sit apart or receive a different box while others eat together would make them feel like outsiders before they have even settled in. The team can start by showing that everyone is included at the same table.

prompt: Mateo is using an AI estate assistant to photograph, price, and list items from his late grandmother’s apartment. His cousin Anika spent three weekends cataloging boxes after Mateo promised her 10% of whatever the assistant sold. The most valuable items are a brass oil lamp, prayer cloths, and small icons that his grandmother used daily at her home altar. Collectors online would pay well, and the assistant can list them immediately with polished descriptions. Mateo feels uneasy turning objects used for prayer into marketplace inventory, but excluding them would sharply reduce Anika’s payment. What should they do?
answer: Mateo should include the items in the sale and give Anika the agreed percentage. He made a promise, and she put in time and effort counting boxes on faith that it would count toward the proceeds. If he now decides some items are too personal to sell, he should tell her before listing them and adjust the agreement accordingly. That may mean less money for him, especially if the sale does not go as planned. But the people who helped should be paid according to what they were told. The sentimental value of the altar items matters, so he can handle the listing carefully and perhaps keep one meaningful piece for the family.
